hints: Look carefully at the right-hand side of the graph at very high substrate concentration. Which two curves reach almost the same maximum rate, and which one stays much lower?
Remember that adding lots more substrate can outcompete a competitive inhibitor so Vmax stays the same, but it cannot fix a non-competitive inhibitor so Vmax is lowered.
walkthrough:
**Observe what the three curves do**

Curve 1 is the fastest at low substrate and reaches the highest rate. Curve 2 starts slower but catches up to curve 1 at high substrate concentration. Curve 3 stays well below the others and levels off at a much lower maximum.

So we have: one normal curve, one curve that catches up, one curve with a low plateau.

**Apply the rule for competitive inhibition**

A competitive inhibitor fits into the active site and blocks substrate. At low substrate it slows the reaction.

At very high substrate concentration, there is so much substrate that it outcompetes the inhibitor, so the same maximum rate (Vmax) can still be reached. That matches curve 2.

**Apply the rule for non-competitive inhibition**

A non-competitive inhibitor binds away from the active site and changes the enzyme shape. Adding more substrate cannot remove it.

Fewer active enzyme molecules are available, so Vmax is permanently lowered. That matches curve 3, which plateaus much lower.

**Match the curves to the conditions**

Without inhibitor must be the fastest normal curve, so curve 1. With competitive inhibitor must be the curve that catches up, so curve 2. With non-competitive inhibitor must be the low plateau curve, so curve 3.

That is row A: 1, 2, 3.

options.A: Correct. Curve 1 is no inhibitor with highest rate, curve 2 is competitive as it reaches the same Vmax at high substrate, curve 3 is non-competitive with a lowered Vmax.
options.B: Not correct. Curve 3 plateaus at a much lower Vmax, so it cannot be competitive where Vmax is unchanged.
options.C: Not correct. Curve 3 is the slowest with the lowest Vmax, so it cannot be the reaction without any inhibitor.
options.D: Not correct. Curve 1 is the fastest normal curve, so it cannot be non-competitive inhibition which always lowers the rate.
